First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{2}{e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}]}_{a}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{e}^{2x}]}_{a}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{4}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{2x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{2x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14047719/assets/b350aaef1440524297a84168de46be1171b7686d9937ef5bbfc5cd55835ea54f.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{2}{e}^{2x} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{4}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ({e}^{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
